abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of long-term neurological impairments and is associated with persistent neuroinflammation. Multicellular nodules, composed of densely aggregated myeloid cells, have been reported in human post-mortem tissue following TBI but remain poorly characterized. Here, we utilized a clinically relevant porcine model of closed-head diffuse TBI generated through rotational acceleration to characterize the temporal and spatial distribution of these nodules. Nodules were rare in sham animals and minimally present at acute time points but increased significantly by 14 days post injury. Nodule burden increased as a function of injury severity and was positively correlated with rotational injury velocity. Nodules were enriched within white matter structures, including subcortical white matter, corpus callosum, fornix, and internal capsule, while remaining minimally present in cortical gray matter. Within these regions, nodules exhibited a widespread yet spatially organized distribution rather than local clustering around a single anatomical location. Together, these findings demonstrate that multicellular nodules are a robust and reproducible neuroinflammatory pathology following diffuse TBI in a gyrencephalic large-animal model. By establishing the temporal progression, severity dependence, and white matter enrichment of this clinically relevant but understudied endophenotype, this work provides a foundation for future investigations into the mechanisms and consequences of post-traumatic neuroinflammation.
